summary: This work demonstrates error suppression in quantum simulations on IBM's superconducting quantum processors by encoding logical qubits in the [[4,2,2]] Iceberg code and performing partially fault-tolerant syndrome extraction. Using 21 code blocks to simulate 42 logical qubits on ibm_boston, encoded simulations of the Ising model achieve 2–6% improvement in local observable accuracy over unencoded runs in 1D and over 200% improvement in 2D, with performance gains growing with circuit depth in higher dimensions.
motivation: Near-term quantum computers suffer from errors that accumulate during quantum simulations, limiting the systems that can be faithfully simulated. This work explores whether lightweight error detection codes can suppress errors in NISQ devices operating near the pseudothreshold, combining fault-tolerant syndrome extraction with non-fault-tolerant logical operations to balance error suppression against circuit overhead.
method: The authors implement the [[4,2,2]] code with fault-tolerant syndrome extraction and non-fault-tolerant logical rotations on heavy-hex connectivity, using simulated annealing to optimize block placement for square-grid logical connectivity. They introduce Observable-Ranked Postselection (ORP), which selectively filters detection events based on syndrome correlations to recover reliable results without exponential shot loss, and validate performance through tensor-network simulations of false-vacuum decay in the Mixed-Field Ising model.
result: Encoded 1D simulations achieve median absolute error reduction of up to 36.1% with $R=1$ syndrome extraction round; in 2D, the signal-survival factor $\alpha$ exceeds unencoded values at all times, with encoding improvement averaging $23.5\pm0.8\%$ per unit time and reaching >200% at late times, driven by the reduced geometric overhead of encoding relative to direct unencoded embedding of 2D lattices on heavy-hex hardware.
